### <span id="page-68-1"></span><span id="page-68-0"></span>**4.7 Enabling the distribution of interrupts**

The following control bits enable and disable the distribution of interrupts:

- [GICD\\_CTLR.](#page-543-0)EnableGrp1S.
- [GICD\\_CTLR.](#page-543-0)EnableGrp1NS.
- [GICD\\_CTLR.](#page-543-0)EnableGrp0.

The following control bits enable and disable the distribution of interrupt groups at the CPU interface:

- [ICC\\_IGRPEN0\\_EL1.](#page-256-0)Enable for Group 0 interrupts.
- [ICC\\_IGRPEN1\\_EL1.](#page-259-0)Enable for Group 1 interrupts.

**Note**

There is a Secure and a Non-secure copy of this register.

• [ICC\\_IGRPEN1\\_EL3.](#page-262-0){EnableGrp1S, EnableGrp1NS}.

Physical LPIs are enabled by a write to [GICR\\_CTLR](#page-640-0).EnableLPIs.

#### **4.7.1 Enabling individual interrupts**

**PPIs**

PPIs can be enabled and disabled by writing to [GICR\\_ISENABLER0](#page-687-0) and [GICR\\_ICENABLER0](#page-648-0) when affinity routing is enabled for the Security state of the interrupt. Individual PPIs can also be enabled and disabled by writing to [GICD\\_ISENABLER<n>](#page-592-0) and [GICD\\_ICENABLER<n>.](#page-553-0) *n* = 0 for PPIs, if legacy operation for physical interrupts is supported and configured.

PPIs in the OPTIONAL, extended PPI range are enabled and disabled by writing to [GICR\\_ISENABLER<n>E,](#page-689-0) and [GICD\\_ICENABLER<n>E](#page-555-0).

**SPIs**

Individual SPIs can be enabled and disabled by writing to [GICD\\_ISENABLER<n>](#page-592-0) and [GICD\\_ICENABLER<n>.](#page-553-0) *n* >0 for SPIs.

SPIs in the OPTIONAL, extended SPI range are enabled and disabled by writing to [GICD\\_ISENABLER<n>E](#page-594-0), and [GICD\\_ICENABLER<n>E.](#page-555-0)

**SGIs**

SGIs can be enabled and disabled by writing to [GICR\\_ISENABLER0](#page-687-0) and [GICR\\_ICENABLER0](#page-648-0) when affinity routing is enabled. Individual SGIs can also be enabled and disabled by writing to [GICD\\_ISENABLER<n>](#page-592-0) and [GICD\\_ICENABLER<n>.](#page-553-0) *n* = 0 for SGIs, if legacy operation for physical interrupts is supported and configured.

**Note**

Whether SGIs are permanently enabled, or can be enabled and disabled by writes to [GICR\\_ISENABLER0](#page-687-0) and [GICR\\_ICENABLER0](#page-648-0), is IMPLEMENTATION DEFINED.

**LPIs**

Individual LPIs can be enabled by setting the enable bits programmed in the LPI Configuration table. For more information about enabling LPIs using the LPI Configuration tables, see *[LPI](#page-88-0)  [Configuration tables on page](#page-88-0) 5-89*.

#### **4.7.2 Interaction of group and individual interrupt enables**

The GICD\_\* and GICR\_\* registers determine, at any moment in time, the highest priority pending interrupt that the hardware is aware of for each target PE. This interrupt is presented to the CPU interface of a PE to evaluate whether it is to be signaled to the PE. The enabling of the interrupts affects this evaluation as follows:

• A pending interrupt that is individually disabled in the GICD\_\* or GICR\_\* registers is not one which is considered in the determination of the highest priority pending interrupt, and so cannot be signaled to the PE.

- A pending interrupt that is individually enabled in the GICD\_\* or GICR\_\* registers, but is a member of a group that is disabled in [GICD\\_CTLR](#page-543-0), is not one that is considered in the determination of the highest priority pending interrupt, and so cannot be signaled to the PE.
- A pending 1 of N interrupt that is individually enabled in the GICD\_\* registers and is a member of a group that is enabled in [GICD\\_CTLR](#page-543-0), but is a member of a group that is disabled in [ICC\\_IGRPEN0\\_EL1,](#page-256-0) [ICC\\_IGRPEN1\\_EL1,](#page-259-0) or [ICC\\_IGRPEN1\\_EL3](#page-262-0) for a PE, cannot be selected for that PE. Such an interrupt is not considered in the determination of the highest priority pending interrupt and so cannot be signaled to the PE.
- For a pending direct interrupt that is individually enabled in the GICD\_\* or GICR\_\* registers and is a member of a group that is enabled in [GICD\\_CTLR](#page-543-0), but is a member of a group that is disabled in [ICC\\_IGRPEN0\\_EL1,](#page-256-0) [ICC\\_IGRPEN1\\_EL1,](#page-259-0) or [ICC\\_IGRPEN1\\_EL3](#page-262-0), it is IMPLEMENTATION DEFINED whether or not the interrupt is considered in the determination of the highest priority pending interrupt. If it is determined to be the highest priority pending interrupt, the interrupt is not signaled to the PE, but will mask a lower priority pending interrupt that is a member of a group that is enabled in [ICC\\_IGRPEN0\\_EL1,](#page-256-0) [ICC\\_IGRPEN1\\_EL1,](#page-259-0) or [ICC\\_IGRPEN1\\_EL3](#page-262-0).

LPIs are enabled individually in the LPI Configuration tables, see *[LPI Configuration tables on page](#page-88-0) 5-89*.

#### **4.7.3 Effect of disabling interrupts**

Disabling an interrupt by writing to the appropriate [GICD\\_ICENABLER<n>](#page-553-0) or to [GICR\\_ICENABLER0](#page-648-0), or by writing to the LPI Configuration tables, does not prevent that interrupt from changing state, for example from becoming pending. When [GICR\\_CTLR.](#page-640-0)EnableLPIs == 0, LPIs are never set pending.

If [GICD\\_CTLR.](#page-543-0)EnableGrp0, [GICD\\_CTLR.](#page-543-0)EnableGrp1S, and [GICD\\_CTLR](#page-543-0).EnableGrp1NS are all cleared to 0, it is IMPLEMENTATION DEFINED whether:

- An edge-triggered interrupt signal moves the interrupt to the pending state.
- SGIs can be set pending by writing to [GICD\\_SGIR](#page-611-0), [ICC\\_SGI0R\\_EL1,](#page-272-0) [ICC\\_SGI1R\\_EL1,](#page-275-0) or [ICC\\_ASGI1R\\_EL1](#page-222-0).

If an interrupt is pending on a CPU interface when the corresponding [GICD\\_CTLR.](#page-543-0)EnableGrp0, [GICD\\_CTLR.](#page-543-0)EnableGrp1NS, or [GICD\\_CTLR.](#page-543-0)EnableGrp1S bit is written from 1 to 0, then the interrupt must be retrieved from the CPU interface.

| Note                                                                                   |  |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--|
| This might have no effect on the forwarded interrupt if it has already been activated. |  |

If an interrupt is pending on a CPU interface when software writes [ICC\\_IGRPEN0\\_EL1](#page-256-0).Enable, [ICC\\_IGRPEN0\\_EL1,](#page-256-0) [ICC\\_IGRPEN1\\_EL1](#page-259-0).Enable, or [ICC\\_IGRPEN1\\_EL3](#page-262-0).Enable from 1 to 0, the interrupt must be released by the CPU interface to allow the Distributor to forward the interrupt to a different PE.

### <span id="page-70-1"></span><span id="page-70-0"></span>**4.8 Interrupt prioritization**

This section describes interrupt prioritization in the GIC architecture. Prioritization describes the:

- Configuration and control of interrupt priority.
- Order of execution of pending interrupts.
- Determination of when interrupts are visible to a target PE, including:
  - Interrupt priority masking.
  - Priority grouping.
  - Preemption of an active interrupt.

<span id="page-70-2"></span>Software configures interrupt prioritization in the GIC by assigning a priority value to each interrupt source. Priority values are an 8-bit unsigned binary number. A GIC implementation that supports two Security states must implement a minimum of 32 and a maximum of 256 levels of physical priority. A GIC implementation that supports only a single Security state must implement a minimum of 16 and a maximum of 256 levels of physical priority. If the GIC implements fewer than 256 priority levels, the low-order bits of the priority fields are RAZ/WI. This means that the number of implemented priority field bits is IMPLEMENTATION DEFINED, in the range 4-8. [Table](#page-70-2) 4-9 on [page](#page-70-2) 4-71 shows the relation between the priority field bits and the number of priority levels supported by an implementation.

**Implemented priority bits Possible priority field values Number of priority levels** [7:0] 0x00-0xFF (0-255), all values 256 [7:1] 0x00-0xFE, (0-254), even values only 128 [7:2] 0x00-0xFC (0-252), in steps of 4 64 [7:3] 0x00-0xF8 (0-248), in steps of 8 32 [7:4] 0x00-0xF0 (0-240), in steps of 16 16

**Table 4-9 Effect of not implementing some priority field bits**

In the GIC prioritization scheme, lower numbers have higher priority. This means that the lower the assigned priority value, the higher the priority of the interrupt. Priority field value 0 always indicates the highest possible interrupt priority, and the lowest priority value depends on the number of implemented priority levels.

The [GICD\\_IPRIORITYR<n>](#page-579-0) registers hold the priority value for each supported SPI. An implementation might reserve an SPI for a particular purpose and assign a fixed priority to that interrupt, meaning the priority value for that interrupt is read-only. For other SPIs the [GICD\\_IPRIORITYR<n>](#page-579-0) registers can be written by software to set the interrupt priorities. It is IMPLEMENTATION DEFINED whether a write to [GICD\\_IPRIORITYR<n>](#page-579-0) changes the priority of any active SPI.

In a multiprocessor implementation, the [GICR\\_IPRIORITYR<n>](#page-679-0) and [GICR\\_IPRIORITYR<n>E](#page-681-0) registers define the interrupt priority of each SGI and PPI INTID independently for each target PE.

LPI Configuration tables and LPI Pending tables in memory store LPI priority information and pending status, see *[LPI Configuration tables on page](#page-88-0) 5-89* and *[LPI Pending tables on page](#page-89-0) 5-90*.

The GIC security model provides Secure and Non-secure accesses to the interrupt priority settings.The Non-secure accesses can configure interrupts only in the lower priority half of the supported priority values. Therefore, if the GIC implements 32 priority values, Non-secure accesses see only 16 priority values. See *[Software accesses of](#page-79-0)  [interrupt priority on page](#page-79-0) 4-80* for more information.

To determine the number of priority bits implemented for SPIs, software can write 0xFF to a writable [GICD\\_IPRIORITYR<n>](#page-579-0) priority field and read back the value stored.

To determine the number of priority bits implemented for SGIs and PPIs, software can write 0xFF to the [GICR\\_IPRIORITYR<n>](#page-679-0) priority fields, and read back the value stored.

The GIC architecture does not require all PEs in the system to use the same number of priority bits to control interrupt priority.

![](_page_71_Figure_1.jpeg)

Arm recommends that, before checking the priority range in this way:

- For a peripheral interrupt, software first disables the interrupt.
- For an SGI, software first checks that the interrupt is inactive.

If, on a particular CPU interface, multiple pending interrupts have the same priority, and have [sufficient priority](#page-25-1) for the interface to signal them to the PE, it is IMPLEMENTATION DEFINED how the interface selects which interrupt to signal.

GICv3 guarantees that the highest priority, unmasked, enabled interrupt will be delivered to a target PE in finite time.

There is no guarantee that higher priority interrupts will always be taken before lower priority interrupts, although this will generally be the case.

The remainder of this section describes:

- *[Non-secure accesses to register fields for Secure interrupt priorities on page](#page-72-0) 4-73*.
- *[Priority grouping on page](#page-73-0) 4-74*.
- *[System register access to the Active Priorities registers on page](#page-76-0) 4-77*.
- *[Preemption on page](#page-77-0) 4-78*.
- *[Priority masking on page](#page-78-0) 4-79*.
- *[Software accesses of interrupt priority on page](#page-79-0) 4-80*.
- *[Changing the priority of enabled PPIs, SGIs, and SPIs on page](#page-82-0) 4-83*.

#### **4.8.1 NMI prioritization**

GICv3.3 introduces the non-maskable property for SPIs, PPIs and SGIs. Support for GICv3.3 is indicated by [GICD\\_TYPER](#page-617-0).NMI. An interrupt is configured as being an NMI using the [GICD\\_INMIR<n>,](#page-575-0) [GICD\\_INMIR<n>E](#page-577-0), [GICR\\_INMIR0,](#page-671-0) and [GICR\\_INMIR<n>E](#page-673-0) registers.

When [GICD\\_CTLR](#page-543-0).DS == 0, NMIs have the following priorities:

- Secure NMIs have a higher priority than a non-NMI with priority 0x00.
- Non-secure NMIs have the following priority:
  - Higher priority than a non-NMI with priority 0x80.
  - Lower priority than a non-NMI with priority 0x7F.

When [GICD\\_CTLR](#page-543-0).DS == 1, NMIs have a higher priority than a non-NMI with priority 0x00.

GICv3.3 inserts new priority levels into the existing GIC priority space, as shown in Figure 4-[6 on page](#page-72-1) 4-73.

| Secure NMI     |
|----------------|
| 0x00           |
|                |
| …              |
| 0x7F           |
| Non-secure NMI |
| 0x80           |
|                |
| …              |
|                |
| 0xFF           |

**Figure 4-6 GIC interrupt priority space**

<span id="page-72-1"></span>For an INTID configured as non-maskable, GIC[D|R]\_IPRIORITYR<n>{E}.Priority\_x is RES0.

All NMIs belonging to a given Security state have the same priority. The GIC does not provide ordering guarantees between interrupts of the same priority.

| Note |  |
|------|--|
|------|--|

The priority of an interrupt marked as an NMI does not depend on the SCTLR\_ELx.NMI value of the current Exception level or of the target Exception level.

#### <span id="page-72-0"></span>**4.8.2 Non-secure accesses to register fields for Secure interrupt priorities**

When [GICD\\_CTLR](#page-543-0).DS == 0, the GIC supports the use of:

- Group 0 interrupts as Secure interrupts.
- Secure Group 1 interrupts.
- Non-secure Group 1 interrupts.

To support the Armv8 Security model the register fields associated with Secure interrupts are RAZ/WI for Non-secure accesses. In addition, the following rules apply:

#### **For Non-secure access to a priority field in GICx\_IPRIORITYR<n>:**

If the priority field corresponds to a Non-secure Group 1 interrupt in *[Software accesses of interrupt](#page-79-0)  [priority on page](#page-79-0) 4-80*:

- For SPIs, the priority field is determined by [GICD\\_IPRIORITYR<n>](#page-579-0) or [GICD\\_IPRIORITYR<n>E](#page-581-0).
- For PPIs and SGIs, the priority field is determined by [GICR\\_IPRIORITYR<n>](#page-679-0) or [GICR\\_IPRIORITYR<n>E.](#page-681-0)

#### **For Non-secure access to ICC\_PMR\_EL1 and ICC\_RPR\_EL1 when [SCR\\_EL3](#page-29-4).FIQ == 1:**

- If the current priority mask value is in the range of 0x00-0x7F:
  - A read access returns the value 0x00.
    - The GIC ignores a write access to [ICC\\_PMR\\_EL1.](#page-266-0)
- If the current priority mask value is in the range of 0x80-0xFF:
  - A read access returns the Non-secure read of the current value.
  - A write access to [ICC\\_PMR\\_EL1](#page-266-0) succeeds, based on the Non-secure read of the priority mask value written to the register.

| Note                                                                                      |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| This means a Non-secure write cannot set a priority mask value in the range of 0x00-0x7F. |

#### **For Non-secure access to ICC\_PMR\_EL1 and ICC\_RPR\_EL1 when [SCR\\_EL3](#page-29-4).FIQ == 0:**

The Secure, unshifted view applies.

*[AArch64 functions on page](#page-855-0) 13-856* provides pseudocode that describes accesses to the following System registers in a GIC that supports two Security states:

- [ICC\\_PMR\\_EL1.](#page-266-0)
- [ICC\\_RPR\\_EL1.](#page-269-0)

#### <span id="page-73-2"></span><span id="page-73-0"></span>**4.8.3 Priority grouping**

Priority grouping uses the following *Binary Point Registers*:

- [ICC\\_BPR0\\_EL1](#page-225-0) for Group 0 interrupts. This register is available in all GIC implementations.
- A Non-secure copy of [ICC\\_BPR1\\_EL1](#page-228-0) for Non-secure Group 1 interrupts. If an implementation supports two Security states, there is a Secure and a Non-secure copy of this register. If an implementation supports only one Security state, there is only one copy of this register
- A Secure copy of [ICC\\_BPR1\\_EL1](#page-228-0) for Secure Group 1 interrupts. This register is available only in a GIC implementation that supports two Security states.

The Binary Point Registers split a priority value into two fields, the *group priority* and the *subpriority*. When determining preemption, all interrupts with the same group priority are considered to have the same priority, regardless of the subpriority.

Where multiple pending interrupts have the same group priority, the GIC uses the subpriority field to resolve the priority within a group. Where two or more pending interrupts in a group have the same subpriority, how the GIC selects between the interrupts is implementation specific.

The GIC uses the group priority field to determine whether a pending interrupt has sufficient priority to preempt execution on a PE, as follows:

- The value of the group priority field for the interrupt must be lower than the value of the [running priority](#page-25-2) of the PE. The running priority is the group priority of the highest priority active interrupt that has not received a priority drop on that PE.
- The value of the priority for the interrupt must be lower than the value of its priority mask.

[ICC\\_BPR0\\_EL1](#page-225-0) determines the priority grouping of Group 0 interrupts:

- When [ICC\\_CTLR\\_EL3](#page-237-0).CBPR\_EL1S is set to 1, [ICC\\_BPR0\\_EL1](#page-225-0) also determines the priority grouping of Secure Group 1 interrupts.
- When [ICC\\_CTLR\\_EL3](#page-237-0).CBPR\_EL1NS is set to 1, [ICC\\_BPR0\\_EL1](#page-225-0) also determines the priority grouping of Non-secure Group 1 interrupts

[ICC\\_BPR1\\_EL1](#page-228-0) determines the priority of Group 1 interrupts:

- When [ICC\\_CTLR\\_EL3](#page-237-0).CBPR\_EL1S is cleared to 0, the Secure copy of [ICC\\_BPR1\\_EL1](#page-228-0) determines the priority grouping of Secure Group 1 interrupts.
- When [ICC\\_CTLR\\_EL3](#page-237-0).CBPR\_EL1NS is cleared to 0, the Non-secure copy of [ICC\\_BPR1\\_EL1](#page-228-0) determines the priority grouping of Non-secure Group 1 interrupts.

#### **Note**

- When an interrupt is using Non-secure [ICC\\_BPR1\\_EL1,](#page-228-0) the effective binary point value is that stored in the register, minus one, as shown in Table 4-[11 on page](#page-74-1) 4-75. This means that software with no awareness of the effects of interrupt grouping and where two Security states are supported, sees the same priority grouping mechanism, regardless of whether it is running on a PE that is in Secure state or in Non-secure state.
- Priority grouping always operates on the full priority, which is the value that would be visible to a Secure read. This is different from the value that is visible to a Non-secure read of the priority value corresponding to a Non-secure interrupt. See Figure 4-[10 on page](#page-80-0) 4-81 and Figure 4-[11 on page](#page-81-0) 4-82.
- When EL3 is using AArch32, and [ICC\\_MCTLR](#page-424-0).CBPR\_EL1S == 1, accesses to [ICC\\_BPR1](#page-384-0) at EL3 and not in Monitor mode access the state of [ICC\\_BPR0](#page-380-0).

#### **Pseudocode**

The following pseudocode indicates the group priority of the interrupt.

```
// GroupBits()
// ===========
// Returns the priority group field for the current BPR value for the group
bits(8) GroupBits(bits(8) priority, IntGroup group)
    bit cbpr_G1NS = if HaveEL(EL3) then ICC_CTLR_EL3.CBPR_EL1NS else ICC_CTLR_EL1.CBPR;
    bit cbpr_G1S = if HaveEL(EL3) then ICC_CTLR_EL3.CBPR_EL1S else '0';
    if (group == IntGroup_G0 ||
        (group == IntGroup_G1NS && cbpr_G1NS == '1') ||
```

```
(group == IntGroup_G1S && cbpr_G1S == '1')) then
    bpr = UInt(ICC_BPR0_EL1.BinaryPoint);
elsif group == IntGroup_G1S then
    bpr = UInt(ICC_BPR1_EL1S.BinaryPoint);
else
    bpr = UInt(ICC_BPR1_EL1NS.BinaryPoint) -1;
mask = Ones(7-bpr):Zeros(bpr+1);
return priority AND mask;
```

#### <span id="page-76-0"></span>**4.8.4 System register access to the Active Priorities registers**

Physical Group 0 and Group 1 interrupts access different Active Priorities registers, depending on the interrupt group.

For Group 0 interrupts, these registers are [ICC\\_AP0R<n>\\_EL1,](#page-215-0) where n = 0-3:

- If 32 or fewer priority levels are implemented, accesses to [ICC\\_AP0R<n>\\_EL1](#page-215-0), where n = 1-3, are UNDEFINED.
- If more than 32 and fewer than 65 priority levels are implemented, accesses to [ICC\\_AP0R<n>\\_EL1,](#page-215-0) where n = 2-3, are UNDEFINED.

For Group 1 interrupts, these registers are [ICC\\_AP1R<n>\\_EL1,](#page-218-0) where n= 0-3:

- If 32 or fewer priority levels are implemented, accesses to [ICC\\_AP1R<n>\\_EL1](#page-218-0), where n = 1-3, are UNDEFINED.
- If more than 32 and fewer than 65 priority levels are implemented, accesses to [ICC\\_AP1R<n>\\_EL1,](#page-218-0) where n = 2-3, are UNDEFINED.

The content of [ICC\\_AP0R<n>\\_EL1](#page-215-0), Secure [ICC\\_AP1R<n>\\_EL1](#page-218-0), and Non-secure [ICC\\_AP1R<n>\\_EL1](#page-218-0) is IMPLEMENTATION DEFINED. However, a value of all zeros must be consistent with no priorities being active. From GICv3.3, Secure ICC\_AP1R0\_EL1, and Non-secure ICC\_AP1R0\_EL1 include separate fields for recording active Non-maskable priorities.

![](_page_76_Picture_11.jpeg)

SCTR\_ELx.NMI.

Writing any value other than the last read value, or all zeros, to these registers can cause:

- Interrupts that would otherwise preempt execution to not preempt execution.
- Interrupts that otherwise would not preempt execution to preempt execution.

A Non-secure write to Non-secure [ICC\\_AP1R<n>\\_EL1](#page-218-0) cannot prevent the correct prioritization and cannot prevent the forwarding of interrupts of higher priority than those in the Non-secure priority range.

Writes to these registers in any order other than the following can result in UNPREDICTABLE behavior:

- 1. [ICC\\_AP0R<n>\\_EL1](#page-215-0).
- 2. Secure [ICC\\_AP1R<n>\\_EL1](#page-218-0).
- 3. Non-secure [ICC\\_AP1R<n>\\_EL1](#page-218-0).

**Note**

An ISB is not required between each write to [ICC\\_AP0R<n>\\_EL1,](#page-215-0) Secure [ICC\\_AP1R<n>\\_EL1,](#page-218-0) and Non-secure [ICC\\_AP1R<n>\\_EL1](#page-218-0).

#### <span id="page-77-3"></span><span id="page-77-0"></span>**4.8.5 Preemption**

A CPU interface supports signaling of higher priority pending interrupts to a target PE before an active interrupt completes. A pending interrupt is only signaled if one of the following is true:

- The highest priority pending interrupt is not an NMI and both of the following are true:
  - Its priority is higher than the priority mask for that CPU interface. See *[Priority masking on page](#page-78-0) 4-79*.
  - Its group priority is higher than that of the [running priority](#page-25-2) on the CPU interface. See *[Priority grouping](#page-73-0) [on page](#page-73-0) 4-74* for more information.
- The highest priority pending interrupt is an NMI and one of the following are true:
  - The highest priority pending interrupt is not masked by the PMR. See *[Priority masking on page](#page-78-0) 4-79*.
  - The group priority of the highest priority pending interrupt is higher than the [running priority](#page-25-2).
  - The group priority of the highest priority pending interrupt is equal to the [running priority](#page-25-2), and ICC\_AP1R0\_EL1.NMI is 0 for the Security state owning the interrupt.

![](_page_77_Figure_16.jpeg)

If GICv3.3 is not implemented, then no interrupts are NMIs.

Preemption occurs at the time when the PE takes the new interrupt, and starts handling the new interrupt instead of the previously active interrupt or the currently running process. When this occurs, the initial active interrupt is said to have been *preempted*.

![](_page_78_Picture_1.jpeg)

The value of the I, F, and ALLINT bit in the Process State, [PSTATE](#page-28-3), and the Exception level and the interrupt routing controls in software and hardware, determine whether the PE responds to the signaled interrupt by taking the interrupt. For more information, see *Arm® Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile architecture*.

For more information about enabling interrupts, see *[Enabling the distribution of interrupts on page](#page-68-1) 4-69*.

#### **Preemption level control**

[ICC\\_BPR0\\_EL1](#page-225-0) determines whether a Group 0 interrupt is signaled to the PE for possible preemption. In addition:

- When [ICC\\_CTLR\\_EL3.](#page-237-0)CBPR\_EL1NS == 1, [ICC\\_BPR0\\_EL1](#page-225-0) also determines whether a Non-secure Group 1 interrupt is signaled to the PE for possible preemption.
- When [ICC\\_CTLR\\_EL3](#page-237-0).CBPR\_EL1S == 1, [ICC\\_BPR0\\_EL1](#page-225-0) also determines whether a Secure Group 1 interrupt is signaled to the PE for possible preemption.

[ICC\\_BPR1\\_EL1](#page-228-0) determines whether a Group 1 interrupt is signaled to the PE for possible preemption. The Non-secure copy of this register is used for Non-secure Group 1 interrupts. The Secure copy is used for Secure Group 1 interrupts.

When [ICC\\_CTLR\\_EL3](#page-237-0).CBPR\_EL1NS is set to 1:

- EL3 can write to [ICC\\_BPR1\\_EL1\\_](#page-228-0)NS.
  - When EL3 is using AArch64 state, accesses to [ICC\\_BPR1\\_EL1\\_](#page-228-0)NS from EL3 are not affected by [ICC\\_CTLR\\_EL3.](#page-237-0)CBPR\_EL1NS.
  - When EL3 is using AArch32 state, accesses to [ICC\\_BPR1\\_EL1](#page-228-0)\_NS from Monitor mode are not affected by [ICC\\_CTLR\\_EL3.](#page-237-0)CBPR\_EL1NS.
- Non-secure writes to [ICC\\_BPR1\\_EL1](#page-228-0) at EL1 or EL2 are ignored.
- Non-secure reads of [ICC\\_BPR1\\_EL1](#page-228-0) at EL1 or EL2 return the value of [ICC\\_BPR0\\_EL1](#page-225-0) +1, saturating at 7.

When [ICC\\_CTLR\\_EL3](#page-237-0).CBPR\_EL1S is set to 1:

- Secure reads of [ICC\\_BPR1\\_EL1](#page-228-0) return the value of [ICC\\_BPR0\\_EL1.](#page-225-0)
- Secure writes to [ICC\\_BPR1\\_EL1](#page-228-0) update [ICC\\_BPR0\\_EL1.](#page-225-0)

#### <span id="page-78-0"></span>**4.8.6 Priority masking**

The *Priority Mask Register* for a CPU interface, [ICC\\_PMR\\_EL1](#page-266-0), defines a priority threshold for the target PE. The highest pending interrupt is masked by [ICC\\_PMR\\_EL1](#page-266-0) when either of the following is true:

- The interrupt is not an NMI and the interrupt priority is equal to or lower than [ICC\\_PMR\\_EL1.](#page-266-0)Priority.
- [GICD\\_CTLR.](#page-543-0)DS is 0 and either of the following is true:
  - The interrupt is a Non-secure NMI and [ICC\\_PMR\\_EL1](#page-266-0).Priority is set to a priority in the Secure range.
  - The interrupt is a Non-secure NMI, the current Security state is Secure or Root, and [ICC\\_PMR\\_EL1.](#page-266-0)Priority is set to 0x80.

When [GICD\\_CTLR](#page-543-0).DS is 0, Secure NMIs are never masked by [ICC\\_PMR\\_EL1](#page-266-0). When [GICD\\_CTLR.](#page-543-0)DS is 1, NMIs are never masked by [ICC\\_PMR\\_EL1](#page-266-0).

| Note                                                        |  |  |
|-------------------------------------------------------------|--|--|
| If GICv3.3 is not implemented, then no interrupts are NMIs. |  |  |

The GIC only signals pending interrupts that have a higher priority than this priority threshold to the target PE. A value of zero, the register reset value, masks all interrupts from being signaled to the associated PE. The GIC does not use priority grouping when comparing the priority of a pending interrupt with the priority threshold.

The GIC always masks an interrupt that has the lowest supported priority. This priority is sometimes referred to as the [idle priority](#page-24-3).

![](_page_79_Figure_1.jpeg)

Writing 0xFF to [ICC\\_PMR\\_EL1](#page-266-0) always sets it to the lowest supported priority. Table 4-[9 on page](#page-70-2) 4-71 shows how the lowest supported priority varies with the number of implemented priority bits.

If the GIC provides support for two Security states, [ICC\\_PMR\\_EL1](#page-266-0) is RAZ/WI to Non-secure accesses, if bit[7] == 0. During normal operation, software executing in Non-secure state does not access [ICC\\_PMR\\_EL1w](#page-266-0)hen it is programmed with such a value.

For information that relates to different GIC configurations, see *[Non-secure accesses to register fields for Secure](#page-72-0)  [interrupt priorities on page](#page-72-0) 4-73*.

#### <span id="page-79-3"></span><span id="page-79-0"></span>**4.8.7 Software accesses of interrupt priority**

This section describes Secure and Non-secure reads of interrupt priority, and the relationship between them. It also describes writes to the priority value fields.

![](_page_79_Figure_7.jpeg)

This section applies to any GIC implementation that supports two Security states.

When a PE reads the priority value of a Non-secure Group 1 interrupt, the GIC returns either the Secure or the Non-secure read of that value, depending on whether the access is Secure or Non-secure.

The GIC implements a minimum of 32 and a maximum of 256 priority levels. This means it implements 5-8 bits of the 8-bit priority value fields in the appropriate [GICR\\_IPRIORITYR<n>](#page-679-0) and [GICD\\_IPRIORITYR<n>](#page-579-0) register. All of the implemented priority bits can be accessed by a Secure access, and unimplemented low-order bits of the priority fields are RAZ/WI. [Figure](#page-79-1) 4-7 shows the Secure read of a priority value field for an interrupt. The priority value stored in the Distributor is equivalent to the Secure read.

![](_page_79_Figure_11.jpeg)

**Figure 4-7 Secure read of the priority field for any interrupt**

<span id="page-79-1"></span>In this view:

- Bits H-D are the bits that the GIC must implement, corresponding to 32 priority levels.
- Bits C-A are the bits the GIC might implement. They are RAZ/WI if not implemented.
- The GIC must implement bits H-A to provide the maximum 256 priority levels.

For Non-secure accesses, the GIC supports half the priority levels it supports for Secure accesses, which means a minimum of 16 priority levels. [Figure](#page-79-2) 4-8 shows the Non-secure view of a priority value field for a Non-secure Group 1 interrupt.

![](_page_79_Figure_18.jpeg)

**Figure 4-8 Non-secure read of the priority field for a Non-secure Group 1 interrupt**

<span id="page-79-2"></span>In this read:

- Bits G-D are the bits that the GIC must implement, corresponding to 16 priority levels.
- Bits C-A are the bits the GIC might implement, that are RAZ/WI if not implemented.
- The GIC must implement bits G-A to provide the maximum 128 priority levels.
- Bit [0] is RAZ/WI.

The Non-secure read of a priority value does not show how the value is stored in the registers in the Distributor. For Non-secure writes to a priority field of a Non-secure Group 1 interrupt, before storing the value:

- The value is right-shifted by one bit.
- Bit [7] of the value is set to 1.

This translation means the priority value for the Non-secure Group 1 interrupt is in the bottom half of the priority range.

A Secure read of the priority value for an interrupt returns the value stored in the Distributor. [Figure](#page-80-1) 4-9 shows this Secure read of the priority value field for a Non-secure Group 1 interrupt that has had its priority value field set by a Non-secure access, or has had a priority value with bit[7] == 1 set by a Secure access:

![](_page_80_Figure_6.jpeg)

**Figure 4-9 Secure read of the priority field for a Non-secure Group 1 interrupt**

<span id="page-80-1"></span>A Secure write to the priority value field for a Non-secure Group 1 interrupt can set bit [7] to 0. If a Secure write sets bit[7] to 0:

- A Non-secure read returns the value GFEDCBA0.
- A Non-secure write can change the value of the field, but only to a value that has bit [7] set to 1 for the Secure read of the field.

**Note**

- This behavior of Non-secure accesses applies only to the priority value fields in [GICR\\_IPRIORITYR<n>](#page-679-0) and [GICD\\_IPRIORITYR<n>](#page-579-0), as appropriate:
  - If the Priority field in [ICC\\_PMR\\_EL1](#page-266-0) holds a value with bit [7] == 0, then the field is RAZ/WI for Non-secure accesses.
  - If the Priority field in [ICC\\_RPR\\_EL1](#page-269-0) holds a value with bit [7] == 0, then the field is RAZ for Non-secure reads.
- Arm does not recommend setting bit[7] to 0 for a Non-secure Group 1 interrupt in this way because it places the interrupt in the wrong half of the priority range for maintenance by Non-secure code.

[Figure](#page-80-0) 4-10 shows the relationship between the reads of the priority value fields for Non-secure Group 1 interrupts.

![](_page_80_Figure_17.jpeg)

<span id="page-80-0"></span>**Figure 4-10 Relationship between Secure and Non-secure reads of interrupt priority fields**

[Figure](#page-81-0) 4-11 shows how software reads of the interrupt priorities from Secure and Non-secure accesses relate to the priority values held in the Distributor, and to the interrupt values that are visible to Secure and Non-secure accesses. [Figure](#page-81-0) 4-11 applies to a GIC that implements the maximum range of priority values.

![](_page_81_Figure_2.jpeg)

- a. All priority values are even (bit [0] == 0) in the software view of Non-secure accesses.
- b. Ranges recommended by Arm.

**Figure 4-11 Software reads of the priorities of Group 1 and Group 0 interrupts**

<span id="page-81-0"></span>Table 4-[16 on page](#page-81-1) 4-82 shows how the number of priority value bits implemented by the GIC affects the Secure and Non-secure reads of the priority of a Non-secure Group 1 interrupt.

**Note**

<span id="page-81-1"></span>Software executing in Non-secure state has no visibility of the priority settings of Group 0 interrupts, or where applicable, of Secure Group 1 interrupts.

**Table 4-16 Effect of not implementing some priority field bits, two Security states**

| Implemented priority bits, | Possible priority field values, for a Non-secure Group 1 interrupt |                                     |  |
|----------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------|--|
| as seen by a Secure read   | Secure read                                                        | Non-secure read                     |  |
| [7:0]                      | 0xFF-0x00 (255-0), all values                                      | 0xFE-0x00 (254-0), even values only |  |
| [7:1]                      | 0xFE-0x00 (254-0), even values only                                | 0xFC-0x00 (252-0), in steps of 4    |  |
| [7:2]                      | 0xFC-0x00 (252-0), in steps of 4                                   | 0xF8-0x00 (248-0), in steps of 8    |  |
| [7:3]                      | 0xF8-0x00 (248-0), in steps of 8                                   | 0xF0-0x00 (240-0), in steps of 16   |  |

This model for the presentation of priority values ensures software written to operate with an implementation of this GIC architecture functions as intended regardless of whether the GIC provides support for two Security states. However, programmers must ensure that software assigns the appropriate priority levels to the Group 0 and Group 1 interrupts.

**Note**

To control priority values, Arm strongly recommends that:

- For a Group 0 interrupt, software sets bit[7] of the priority value field to 0.
- If using a Secure write to set the priority of a Non-secure Group 1 interrupt, software sets bit[7] of the priority value field to 1.

This ensures that all Group 0 and, if applicable, Secure Group 1 interrupts have higher priorities than all Non-secure Group 1 interrupts. However, a system might have requirements that cannot be met with this scheme.

[Table](#page-82-1) 4-17 shows an example priority allocation scheme that ensures:

- Some Group 0 interrupts have higher priority than any other interrupts.
- <span id="page-82-1"></span>• Some Secure Group 1 interrupts have higher priority than any Non-secure Group 1 interrupt.

**Table 4-17 Example priority allocation**

| Interrupt security configuration | GICR_IPRIORITYR <n>[7:6]</n> |
|----------------------------------|------------------------------|
| Group 0                          | 0b00                         |
| Secure Group 1                   | 0b01                         |
| Non-secure Group 1               | 0b10<br>0b11                 |

- Software might not be aware that the GIC supports two Security states, and therefore might not know whether it is making Secure or Non-secure accesses to GIC registers. However, for any implemented interrupt, software can write 0xFF to the corresponding [GICR\\_IPRIORITYR<n>](#page-679-0) priority value field, and then read back the value stored in the field to determine the supported interrupt priority range. Arm recommends that, before checking the priority range in this way:
  - For a peripheral interrupt, software first disables the interrupt.
  - For an SGI, software first checks that the interrupt is inactive.

#### <span id="page-82-0"></span>**4.8.8 Changing the priority of enabled PPIs, SGIs, and SPIs**

If software writes to the [GICD\\_IPRIORITYR<n>,](#page-579-0) [GICD\\_IPRIORITYR<n>E,](#page-581-0) [GICR\\_IPRIORITYR<n>](#page-679-0) and [GICR\\_IPRIORITYR<n>E](#page-681-0) registers of an enabled interrupt while the interrupt is pending, it is IMPLEMENTATION DEFINED whether the GIC uses the old value or the new value. The GIC ensures that no interrupt is handled more than once, and that no interrupt is lost. The effect of the write must be visible in finite time.

## <span id="page-84-1"></span><span id="page-84-0"></span>Chapter 5

## **Locality-specific Peripheral Interrupts and the ITS**

This chapter describes *Locality-specific Peripheral Interrupts* (LPIs) and the *Interrupt Translation Service* (ITS). It contains the following sections:

- *[LPIs on page](#page-85-1) 5-86*.
- *[The Interrupt Translation Service on page](#page-91-1) 5-92*.
- *[ITS commands on page](#page-100-1) 5-101*.
- *[Common ITS pseudocode functions on page](#page-135-1) 5-136*.
- *[ITS command error encodings on page](#page-145-1) 5-146*.
- *[ITS power management on page](#page-148-1) 5-149*.

#### <span id="page-85-1"></span><span id="page-85-0"></span>**5.1 LPIs**

*Locality-specific Peripheral Interrupts* (LPIs) are edge-triggered message-based interrupts that can use an *Interrupt Translation Service* (ITS), if it is implemented, to route an interrupt to a specific Redistributor and connected PE. GICv3 provides two types of support for LPIs. LPIs can be supported either:

- Using the ITS to translate an EventID from a device into an LPI INTID. For more information about EventIDs, see *[The Interrupt Translation Service on page](#page-91-1) 5-92*.
- By forwarding an LPI INTID directly to the Redistributors, using [GICR\\_SETLPIR](#page-705-0).

An implementation must support only one of these methods.

![](_page_85_Picture_6.jpeg)

The following registers are mandatory in an implementation that supports LPIs but does not include an ITS:

- [GICR\\_INVLPIR.](#page-677-0)
- [GICR\\_INVALLR.](#page-675-0)
- [GICR\\_SYNCR](#page-709-0).

Support for these registers is IMPLEMENTATION DEFINED in implementations that do include an ITS.

These registers control physical LPIs in a system that does not include an ITS:

- [GICR\\_SETLPIR.](#page-705-0)
- [GICR\\_CLRLPIR](#page-638-0).

In an implementation that includes LPIs, at least 8192 LPIs are supported. For this reason, the configuration of each interrupt, and the pending information for each interrupt, is held in tables in memory, rather than in registers, and the tables are pointed to by registers held in the Redistributors.

- **Note** Arm expects that an implementation will cache parts of the tables in the Redistributors to reduce latency and memory traffic. The form of these caches is IMPLEMENTATION DEFINED.
- When the GIC supports two Security states, the addresses for the LPI tables are in the Non-secure physical address space.

Figure 5-[1 on page](#page-86-0) 5-87 shows the generation of LPIs in an implementation that includes at least one ITS.

![](_page_86_Figure_1.jpeg)

a. There might be zero, one, or more than one ITS in a GIC.

In [Figure](#page-86-0) 5-1, the ITS channel to the Redistributors is IMPLEMENTATION DEFINED.

**Figure 5-1 Triggering LPIs in an implementation with an ITS**

<span id="page-86-0"></span>**Note**

Figure 5-[2 on page](#page-87-0) 5-88 shows the generation of LPIs in an implementation without an ITS.

![](_page_87_Picture_1.jpeg)

**Figure 5-2 Triggering LPIs in an implementation without an ITS**

<span id="page-87-0"></span>When [GICD\\_CTLR](#page-543-0).DS == 0:

- LPIs are only supported when affinity routing is enabled for Non-secure state.
- LPIs are always Non-secure Group 1 interrupts.

When [GICD\\_CTLR](#page-543-0).DS == 1:

- LPIs are only supported when affinity routing is enabled.
- LPIs are always Group 1 interrupts.

There is a single global physical LPI space so that LPIs can be moved between all Redistributors. Software programs the size of the single global physical LPI space using [GICR\\_PROPBASER](#page-702-0).IDbits.

![](_page_87_Picture_10.jpeg)

The size of the physical LPI space is limited to the maximum size that an implementation supports, which is defined in [GICD\\_TYPER.](#page-617-0)IDbits.

For a given Redistributor, LPI configuration and state are maintained in two tables in memory, described in the following sections:

- *[LPI Configuration tables on page](#page-88-1) 5-89*.
- *[LPI Pending tables on page](#page-89-1) 5-90*.

If a Redistributor supports physical LPIs, it has:

• LPI priority and enable bits programmed in the LPI Configuration table. The address of the LPI Configuration table is defined by [GICR\\_PROPBASER.](#page-702-0) If [GICR\\_PROPBASER](#page-702-0) is updated when [GICR\\_CTLR](#page-640-0).EnableLPIs == 1, the effects are UNPREDICTABLE. See *[LPI Configuration tables on page](#page-88-1) 5-89* for more information.

• Memory-backed storage for LPI pending bits in an LPI Pending table. This table is specific to a particular Redistributor. The address of the LPI Pending table is defined by [GICR\\_PENDBASER](#page-699-0). If [GICR\\_PENDBASER](#page-699-0) is updated when [GICR\\_CTLR.](#page-640-0)EnableLPIs == 1, the effects are UNPREDICTABLE.

[GICR\\_PROPBASER.](#page-702-0)IDBits sets the size of the ID space, and thereby the number of entries in the LPI Configuration table and the corresponding LPI Pending table.

Physical LPIs are enabled by a write to [GICR\\_CTLR](#page-640-0).EnableLPIs.

![](_page_88_Picture_4.jpeg)

When LPIs are disabled at the Redistributor interface, that is when [GICR\\_CTLR.](#page-640-0)EnableLPIs == 0, LPIs cannot become pending. An attempt to make an LPI pending in this situation has no effect, and the LPI is lost. This differs from disabling SGIs, PPIs, and SPIs, which prevents only the signaling of the interrupt to the CPU interface.

GICv4 introduces equivalent tables for handling virtual LPIs with addresses referenced in [GICR\\_VPROPBASER](#page-720-0) and [GICR\\_VPENDBASER.](#page-714-0)

In GICv4, virtual LPIs are enabled by a write to [GICR\\_VPENDBASER.](#page-714-0)Valid.

#### <span id="page-88-1"></span><span id="page-88-0"></span>**5.1.1 LPI Configuration tables**

LPI configuration is global. Whether a GIC supports Redistributors that point at different copies of the LPI Configuration table is IMPLEMENTATION DEFINED.

It is IMPLEMENTATION DEFINED whether [GICR\\_PROPBASER](#page-702-0) can be set to different values on different Redistributors. [GICR\\_TYPER.](#page-710-0)CommonLPIAff indicates which Redistributors must have [GICR\\_PROPBASER](#page-702-0) set to the same value whenever [GICR\\_CTLR](#page-640-0).EnableLPIs == 1.

An implementation can treat all copies of [GICR\\_PROPBASER](#page-702-0) that are required to have the same value as accessing common state.

Setting different values in different copies of [GICR\\_PROPBASER](#page-702-0) on Redistributors that are required to use a common LPI Configuration table when [GICR\\_CTLR.](#page-640-0)EnableLPIs == 1 leads to UNPREDICTABLE behavior.

If [GICR\\_PROPBASER](#page-702-0) is programmed to different values on different Redistributors, it is IMPLEMENTATION DEFINED which copy or copies of [GICR\\_PROPBASER](#page-702-0) are used when the GIC reads the LPI Configuration tables. However, the copy or copies that are used will correspond to a Redistributor on which [GICR\\_CTLR.](#page-640-0)EnableLPIs == 1.

To avoid unpredictable behavior, software must ensure that all copies of the LPI Configuration tables are identical, and all changes are globally observable, whenever:

- [GICR\\_CTLR](#page-640-0).EnableLPIs is written from 0 to 1 on any Redistributor.
- [GICR\\_INVLPIR](#page-677-0) and [GICR\\_INVALLR](#page-675-0) are written on any Redistributor with [GICR\\_CTLR.](#page-640-0)EnableLPIs == 1, if direct LPIs are supported.
- The [INV](#page-107-0) and [INVALL](#page-108-0) command is executed by an ITS, in an implementation that includes at least one ITS.

An LPI Configuration table in memory stores entries containing configuration information for each LPI, where:

- [GICR\\_PROPBASER](#page-702-0) specifies a 4KB aligned physical address. This is the LPI Configuration table base address.
- For any LPI N, the location of the table entry is defined by (base address + (N 8192)).

To change the configuration of an interrupt, software writes to the LPI Configuration tables and then issues the [INV](#page-107-0) or [INVALL](#page-108-0) command. In implementations that do not include an ITS, software writes to [GICR\\_INVALLR](#page-675-0) or [GICR\\_INVLPIR.](#page-677-0)

The LPI Configuration table contains an 8-bit entry for each LPI. Figure 5-[3 on page](#page-89-2) 5-90 shows the LPI Configuration table entry format.

![](_page_89_Picture_1.jpeg)

**Figure 5-3 LPI Configuration table entry**

<span id="page-89-3"></span>Table 5-[1 on page](#page-89-3) 5-90 shows the LPI Configuration table entry bit assignments.

**Table 5-1 LPI Configuration table entry bit assignments**

<span id="page-89-2"></span>

| Bits  | Name     | Function                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |  |
|-------|----------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--|
| [7:2] | Priority | The priority of the LPI. These are the most significant bits of the LPI priority. Bits[1:0] of the priority are 0.                                                                                                                                                                                |  |
|       |          | When GICD_CTLR.DS == 0, this value is shifted in accordance with the security and priority rules specified in<br>Software accesses of interrupt priority on page 4-80. This means that LPI priorities are always in the lower half of<br>the priority range. The priority value range is 128-254. |  |
|       |          | If GICD_CTLR.DS == 1, the value in this field is not shifted.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |  |
|       |          | In GICv4, the virtual LPI Configuration tables behave as if GICD_CTLR.DS == 1 and therefore the priority is not<br>shifted.                                                                                                                                                                       |  |
|       |          | Note<br>An implementation might support fewer than 8 bits of priority. Unimplemented bits will be treated as RES0.                                                                                                                                                                                |  |
|       |          | See Interrupt prioritization on page 4-71 for more information about interrupt priorities.                                                                                                                                                                                                        |  |
